stances.claim: Del Castillo is one of the most humble and competent jurists CJ knows -- embodying the constitutional standards of proven competence, integrity, probity, and independence -- and has conducted himself with the rare poise of being 'friendly yet detached; familiar yet objective; strict yet fair; self-assured yet collegial.'
stances.rhetorical_move: personal-tribute portrait (chiastic doublets compressed into a single sentence)

stances.claim: Del Castillo's declining the chief-justiceship after Leonardo-de Castro's retirement -- citing only eight months left and a preference to 'concentrate on my work as an associate justice and as chairman of the 2018 bar exams' -- is the rare self-abnegation of a senior justice who could have had the title.

Despite Del Castillo's modest student record ('while he did not graduate with honors, he did even better'), his career embodies the lesson that a jurist's stature is built through patient, faceless service from the lowest rung of the judicial ladder up.
stances.confidence: asserted with affectionate exception ('he did even better' = he married the class valedictorian)

stances.claim: With Del Castillo's retirement, Duterte appointees will form 8 of 15 SC justices -- a clear majority -- rising to a super-majority of 11 by end of October 2019 after Jardeleza, Bersamin, and Carpio retire, and ultimately to 13 (with the chief) by June 30, 2022, leaving only Leonen and Caguioa from the pre-Duterte court.
stances.rhetorical_move: concession-counting projection (deliberate accounting of an institutional shift)

stances.claim: How a Duterte super-majority will affect SC independence deserves its own column -- but new justices, who 'may feel a debt of gratitude (a deep-rooted Filipino trait) to the appointing authority during their first year in office,' soon learn 'that the temporaries of the moment are always overtaken by the permanencies of history.'
stances.confidence: asserted with characteristic optimism about institutional self-correction

notable_anecdotes: Del Castillo's reason for declining the chief-justiceship -- 'I will be retiring in about eight months, and I don't think I can make a difference as chief justice. I would rather concentrate on my work as an associate justice and as chairman of the 2018 bar exams' -- quoted directly from a private exchange, a vanishingly rare CJ-level act of self-abnegation that the column treats as the single most defining character moment.

The 'while he did not graduate with honors, he did even better' aside -- that Del Castillo 'wooed and convinced Cynthia Roxas, their 1976 class valedictorian at the Ateneo de Manila School of Law, to marry him' -- and 'the couple, like in our favorite fairy tales, lived happily ever after,' with Cynthia later becoming the youngest and first female dean of Ateneo Law. The compressed romance-as-life-arc is the column's emotional center.

The compressed chiastic-doublet portrait -- 'friendly yet detached; familiar yet objective; strict yet fair; self-assured yet collegial' -- four paired oppositions in a single sentence, the densest single-sentence character portrait in this set of columns.
The closing epigram -- 'the temporaries of the moment are always overtaken by the permanencies of history' -- CJ's characteristic optimism that institutional drift can be corrected over generations.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban honors Justice Mariano C. del Castillo, who will be feted by his colleagues on July 26, 2019 -- three days before his 70th birthday on July 29, because the Constitution's 'until they reach the age of seventy' has been interpreted as 'until midnight of the day before' the 70th birthday. He traces Del Castillo's 30-year arc from MTC San Mateo (1989) through RTC Angeles, RTC QC, and the Court of Appeals to the Supreme Court (July 29, 2009), noting that Del Castillo declined his nomination to succeed CJ Leonardo-de Castro in 2018 with the characteristically humble explanation: 'I will be retiring in about eight months, and I don't think I can make a difference as chief justice. I would rather concentrate on my work as an associate justice and as chairman of the 2018 bar exams.' Del Castillo, CJ argues, embodies the constitutional standards of competence, integrity, probity, and independence -- 'friendly yet detached; familiar yet objective; strict yet fair; self-assured yet collegial' -- a gentleman-jurist whose career was modest in honors but rich in substance (his student peak was marrying the 1976 class valedictorian, who later became dean of Ateneo Law). With his retirement, Duterte's appointees rise to 8 of 15; after Jardeleza, Bersamin, and Carpio retire in Sept-Oct 2019, the figure climbs to 11, and by June 30, 2022 to 13 with the chief -- leaving only Leonen and Caguioa from the pre-Duterte court. How this super-majority will affect SC independence deserves a future column, CJ writes, but new justices soon learn 'that the temporaries of the moment are always overtaken by the permanencies of history.'
